faq.a: Palpate the fundus: a firm, non‑compressible area suggests thickened myometrium; a soft, easily indented fundus may indicate thinning.
faq.q: How can I assess upper segment thickness without ultrasound?

faq.a: A firm segment may mean the uterus is not relaxing between contractions, increasing rupture risk; stopping oxytocin reduces stress.
faq.q: Why is oxytocin stopped when the upper segment is firm?

faq.a: If the upper segment remains >2 mm thick and there is no hyper‑stimulation, a trial may be considered, but close monitoring is mandatory.
faq.q: What is the safe interval for a trial of labour after a previous Caesarean?

exam: A woman with one previous low‑segment Caesarean presents in labour; ultrasound shows 1.5 mm upper segment thickness — what is your immediate plan? — Stop uterotonics, give tocolysis, arrange emergency Caesarean.
During oxytocin augmentation, the fundus becomes hard and does not descend — what does this indicate? — Possible uterine rupture; stop oxytocin, assess vitals, prepare for surgery.
Explain how the Bishop score incorporates upper segment behaviour. — Consistency (firm vs. soft) reflects upper segment contractility and predicts induction success.
A patient in obstructed labour has a firm upper segment but a soft lower segment — what is the next step? — Consider operative delivery (Caesarean) as labour is unlikely to progress.
Why is a thin upper segment (<2 mm) more concerning than a low fetal heart rate alone? — Thin segment signals structural failure risk; combined with fetal distress it mandates urgent delivery.
In a low‑resource setting without ultrasound, how would you monitor a scarred uterus for rupture? — Serial palpation of fundal thickness, watch for pain, vitals, and fetal heart patterns.

Differentiate uterine rupture from uterine dehiscence on clinical grounds. — Rupture presents with acute pain, peritoneal signs, and fetal distress; dehiscence may be silent with only mild tenderness.
What pharmacologic agents are avoided in a patient with a firm upper segment and why? — Avoid further uterotonics (oxytocin, ergometrine) as they increase contractile stress and rupture risk.
ai.title: Upper Uterine Segment
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: The upper uterine segment is the contractile part of the uterus above the internal os. Its thickness and integrity are crucial in labour, uterine rupture risk, and surgical decisions, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Upper segment thickness measured by ultrasound predicts uterine rupture risk in scarred uteri.
In low‑resource hospitals, clinical assessment (palpation, fundal height) often substitutes imaging.
sections.p: The uterus is divided into the lower (cervical) and upper (body/fundus) segments by the internal os. The upper segment consists of thick myometrium that contracts during labour and expands during pregnancy.

b: Bishop score includes cervical dilation, effacement, station, consistency, and position; upper segment behaviour underlies consistency.
A thin, over‑distended upper segment (>2 cm thinning) signals impending rupture, especially with previous Caesarean.
sections.p: During labour the upper segment shortens and thickens, while the lower segment thins and stretches. This differential change is the basis of the Bishop score and guides induction decisions.

b: In scarred uterus, monitor for excessive thinning (<2 mm on ultrasound) or loss of contractility.
In obstructed labour, a firm, non‑stretching upper segment suggests failure to progress.
sections.p: Recognition of abnormal upper segment changes prevents catastrophic uterine rupture and guides operative timing.

b: Describe how to palpate upper segment thickness in a labouring woman.
Explain why a firm upper segment after oxytocin infusion may indicate uterine rupture.
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to assess the upper segment clinically and decide management.

t.a: Transabdominal ultrasound measurement of myometrial thickness
t.b: Is the upper segment thinned enough to risk rupture? <2 mm suggests high risk; if unavailable, use fundal height trends and palpation.
Does the uterus contract effectively? Decelerations with a firm upper segment raise suspicion of rupture.

t.a: Maternal vital signs and abdominal exam
t.b: Is there sudden abdominal pain or tenderness indicating rupture? Look for guarding, rigidity, and shock.

b: If upper segment thinning is noted in a scarred uterus, stop uterotonics, give tocolysis (e.g., nifedipine) and prepare for emergency Caesarean.
In obstructed labour with a firm upper segment, consider operative delivery (Caesarean or instrumental) promptly.
Supportive care: IV fluids, blood typing, and analgesia; monitor for hemorrhage.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect the uterus, and monitor mother and fetus.

b: Cervical insufficiency presents with painless dilation, not a firm upper segment.
Placenta previa causes painless bleeding without upper segment thickening.
sections.p: Lower uterine segment pathology such as cervical insufficiency or placenta previa can mimic upper segment issues.

b: A normal‑appearing thickness on a poor‑quality scan may miss focal thinning.
Fetal heart decelerations can be due to cord compression, not uterine rupture.
sections.p: Ultrasound may over‑estimate thickness in dehydrated patients; clinical palpation remains essential.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with a firm, non‑stretching uterus
Maternal hypotension or tachycardia suggesting hemorrhage
Fetal distress (persistent decelerations) with abnormal uterine findings
